L426: Polypropylene (PP) represents the second largest share, accounting for 19% of the global plastics production and thus contributes essentially to primary plastic waste generation [【36†1】, 【37†2】]. The application range of PP spans from short-life packaging to construction products designed to last up to a century.
L427: Over 40% of post-consumer recycled materials used in new products are applied in the building and construction sector, where high durability and mechanical performance are essential and can only be guaranteed by a controlled and consistent recycling quality [【38†3】]. Recycled PP is already widely used in structural applications such as cable trays, stormwater management systems, and drainage infrastructure [【39†4】].
L428: While standards and regulations for PP recycling exist, their adequacy in ensuring consistent recyclate quality remains unproven. A balance between regulatory compliance and industrial feasibility is essential to establish a recycling system that delivers high-quality recyclates for diverse applications.
L429: Several standards specify recycled materials, such as polymers specific (EN 15344 [【40†5】], EN 15345 [【41†6】], EN 15346 [【42†7】], etc.), product related (EN 13430 [【43†8】], EN 13437 [【44†9】], ONR CEN/TS 14541–2 [【45†10】], etc.) and testing standards (ISO 15270 [【46†11】], EN 15343 [【47†12】], CEN/TS 16010 [【48†13】], EN 15347 [【49†14】] etc.). However, many of these allow the use of external reprocessed and recycled materials, but no defined values for specific applications are existing.
L430: For example, in the standard EN 1852–1 [【50†15】] and EN 1451–1 [【51†16】], which define product standards for plastic piping systems, it is stated, “To be agreed between the manufacturer and supplier”, which offers a high degree of freedom. Typically, only basic material properties, such as shape, color, density ρ, melt flow rate (MFR) and impact strength a_{cU} are required. Other parameters, like ash content or polymer composition, are optional.
L431: This yields another problem for proper use of recyclate: the lack of information provided to manufacturers. A study analyzing 51 recycled PP data sheets revealed that sufficient and comprehensible values were provided only for ρ, MFR and a_{cU}, while ash content was reported in only 22 of the data sheets [【52†17】].
L432: Inconsistent and insufficient recyclate quality limits potential applications and restricts the broader use of recycled polymers [【53†18】, 【54†19】]. The quality of recycled materials is thus a key factor for their suitability in high-performance applications. In reality, recyclate quality is affected by both controllable and uncontrollable factors [【55†20】-【56†22】]. Non-controllable factors include the origin of the waste, consumer behavior, and seasonal variations in waste composition.
L433: Additionally, technological advances, regulations, policy changes, and changes in product design also influence the availability and quality of the recycled material [【57†23】-【58†27】].
L434: Beyond feedstock variability, technological advancements in sorting and treatment processes are crucial for achieving optimal recyclate quality. While the composition of the collected plastic waste is only partially controllable, treatment steps like sorting, grinding, washing, drying, and melt filtration can reduce impurities and enhance quality [【59†21】, 【60†28】-【61†30】].
L435: However, contaminations, like homogenic (e.g., various PP grades) or heterogenic (e.g., PE in PP) polymeric and non-polymeric impurities may still be present and negatively affect the performance of recycled materials [【62†31】-【63†35】]. As a result, high purity and quality are difficult to achieve.
L436: Particularly for PP, cross-contamination between PE and PP is critical due to their similar chemical compositions and inherent immiscibility without expensive compatibilizers, which can compromise the integrity and performance of materials in various applications [【64†32】, 【65†36】, 【66†37】].
L437: Thermal and mechanical degradation during use, storage or treatment can further reduce molecular weight and compromise material properties [【59†21】]. This highlights the importance of proper pre-sorting and treatment of waste to achieve consistent and high recyclate quality [【53†18】].
L438: For a better understanding of the extent of quality variations of recyclates, this study analyzed ten batches of a specified post-consumer PP recyclate used in industry over a period of 15 months. The MFR and density ρ, two specifications commonly used in industry, were defined as a benchmark in order to analyze the variation in material properties under realistic conditions.
L439: This approach provides insight into the challenges of ensuring consistent recyclate quality for technically demanding applications and for optimizing recycling processes and industrial standards. In addition to basic material characterization, the core objective was to assess the potential of recycled PP for high-performance applications, where consistent mechanical performance and long-term durability are essential.
L440: Therefore, the cyclic cracked round bar (CRB) test was performed to evaluate the crack resistance under cyclic load, a critical aspect for structural and long-lifetime products. The findings aim to support a more reliable use of recycled PP and to promote its integration into a sustainable circular economy.
L441: ## 2 Experimental
L442: ### 2.1 Material and Sample Preparation

These batches were ordered with identical specifications, aligned with industry requirements for melt flow rate MFR and ρ, as listed in (Table 【67†1】), over the period from August 2021 to November 2022.

L475: ### 2.2 Material Testing
L476: #### 2.2.1 Rheological Analysis
L477: To determine rheological parameters, the single-point value MFR, according to ISO 1133 [【70†38】], was measured using a device from type MFI ITW Instron CEAST (Pianezza, Italien) equipped with a die of 8.0 mm in length and 2.095 mm in diameter. At least ten measurements for each batch were performed on the granules at 230°C and with 2.16 kg.
L478: Additionally, viscosity η as a function of the shear rate $\stackrel{̇}{\gamma }$ and storage modulus G´ and loss modulus G´ over frequency ω were determined using a controlled-stress MCR 302 rheometer (Anton Paar GmbH, Austria) equipped with parallel plates (25 mm diameter and 1 mm gap). Three measurements of each batch were carried out according to ISO 3219-2 [【71†39】] at 230°C, under nitrogen atmosphere on a melt-pressed circular disk with a diameter of 25 mm and a thickness of 1.2 mm.
L479: For the evaluation of the crossover point (intersection of G´ and G´´), G´ and G´´ were measured in oscillation mode, whereas the zero viscosity η_{0} was determined in rotation mode at $\stackrel{̇}{\gamma }$ = 0.001 rad/s.
L480: #### 2.2.2 Fourier-Transform Infrared Spectroscopy
L481: Fourier-Transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) measurements were performed on a SpectrumTwo by PerkinElmer Inc. (Waltham, Massachusetts, USA) in Attenuated Total Reflectance (ATR) mode (Quest ATR unit, Specac Ltd., United Kingdom) with a diamond crystal. For each batch, ten FTIR spectra from the surface of multipurpose specimens were recorded. Each spectrum is an accumulation of four scans from 650 cm^{−1} to 4000 cm^{−1} with a resolution of 4 cm^{−1}.
L482: The normalization and evaluation were done via Spectrum software. Spectra were baseline corrected and peak intensities were normalized using the peak at 2917 cm^{−1} [【72†40】, 【73†41】], which corresponds to alkane CH stretching vibrations of methylene groups [【74†42】]. Then, the mean spectrum of ten spectra was calculated for each batch.
L483: #### 2.2.3 Density and Thermalgravimetric Analysis
L484: 
L485: Density was determined with the immersion method on a Mettler Toledo XS205 Dual Range balance (Mettler-Toledo GmbH, Greifensee, Switzerland) according to ISO 1183-1 [【75†43】]. Five samples, cut out of multipurpose specimens, of each batch were analyzed.
L486: To measure the decomposition temperature and filler content of the batches, following ISO 11358-1 [【76†44】], three samples, of approximately 10 mg for each batch were cut out of multipurpose specimens. The samples were heated up from 35°C up to 850°C with a heating rate of 10°C/min under nitrogen atmosphere with a flow rate of 20 mL/min. For B1-B6 a TGA 8000 of PerkinElmer Inc. (Waltham, Massachusetts, USA) and for B7-B10 a TGA/DSC 3+ (Mettler-Toledo GmbH, Greifensee, Schweiz) were used.
L487: The mass loss from 500°C to 750°C and the ash content at 750°C were evaluated. Between 500°C and 750°C, the mass loss is attributable to the release of gaseous carbon dioxide (CO2) as a result of the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate (CaCO_{3}). The initial CaCO_{3} content ω_{CaCO3} can be calculated by multiplying the mass loss of CO_{2} with the factor 2.27 [【77†45】, 【78†46】].
L488: For determining the talc content ω_{talc}, the remaining calcium oxide CaO content was subtracted from the ash content at 750°C.
L489: #### 2.2.4 Thermal Properties
L490: Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and oxidation onset temperature (OOT) measurements were performed on a DSC 4000 of PerkinElmer Inc. (Waltham, Massachusetts, USA) and evaluated with Pyris Manager software. Three samples of each batch, taken from multipurpose specimens, were used for both DSC and OOT analysis. DSC measurements were performed with a heating rate of 10.00°C/min and nitrogen at a flow rate of 50 mL/min as purge gas, according to ISO 11357-1 [【79†47】].
L491: For further evaluation only the cooling and second heating were taken into account. Results were normalized to the polymer content of each respective batch. This polymer content was calculated by subtracting the average filler content of each batch, evaluated from TGA measurements at 500°C, from the total weight of the sample.
L492: Instead of measuring the oxidation induction time, OOT was determined in accordance with ISO 11357-6 [【80†48】], using the dynamic method under synthetic air (50 mL/min) with a heating rate of 20°C/min, due to its previously published benefits [【81†49】].
L493: #### 2.2.5 Mechanical and Thermo-Mechanical Analysis
L494: Tensile properties were determined according to ISO 527-2 [【82†50】] on a tensile/compression universal testing machine of type Z010 (ZWICK GmbH & Co. KG, Ulm, Germany) with a 10 kN load cell at 23°C. Five injection molded multipurpose specimens of each batch were tested. The Young's modulus E was determined at a test speed of 1 mm/min; subsequently, the test speed was changed to 50 mm/min until failure.
L495: From beginning up to the yield stress σ_{y}, the strain ε was measured by makroXtens II from ZwickRoell GmbH & Co. KG (Ulm, Germany) and then via crosshead.
L496: The unnotched a_{cU} and notched impact strength a_{cN} were examined at room temperature of 23°C with an instrumented pendulum on a ZWICK HIT25P (ZwickRoell GmbH & Co. KG, Ulm, Germany) according to ISO 179-2 [【83†51】]. All specimens, 20 per batch, were taken from multipurpose specimens and tested edgewise. Ten specimens of each batch were notched with a manual notching plane (ZwickRoell GmbH & Co. KG, Ulm, Germany) with notch type A.
L497: The nominal working capacity of the pendulum was 15 J for unnotched and 2 J for notched specimens.
L498: For dynamic-mechanical analysis, samples with a thickness of 1.2–1.5 mm, width of 5–6 mm were manufactured and measured on a DMA Q800 (TA Instruments, New Castle, Delaware, USA). The measuring setup was 3-point bending mode with a support distance of 20 mm and an applied frequency of 1 Hz. The ratio between static and dynamic load was set to 1.25, the dynamic amplitude was 0.05% at a temperature range from −75°C up to 100°C with a heating rate of 3 K/min.
L499: #### 2.2.6 Crack Resistance Under Cyclic Load
L500: In this work, the cyclic Cracked Round Bar (CRB) test was used to characterize the fatigue behavior under cyclic load of the batches. Therefore, a compression molded plate with a thickness of 15 mm was processed and a cylindrical specimen with a diameter of 14 mm and an initial notch depth of 1.4 mm was manufactured.
L501: Measurements were performed following ISO 18489:22015 [【84†52】] at a room temperature of 23°C and an R-ratio (ratio of minimum to maximum force) of 0.1 on a 15 kN servo-hydraulic actuator system (MTS Eden Prairie, MN, USA). To prevent hysteretic heating, the testing frequency was set to 5 Hz [【85†53】-【86†56】]. For each batch, at least six specimens were tested until failure at different applied initial stress intensity factor ΔK_{I,ini} levels from 0.4 MPa·m^{0.5} up to 0.75 MPa·m^{0.5}.
L502: An Axioscope 7 (Carl Zeiss AG, Jena, Germany) optical microscope was used to measure the initial notch depth of the specimen after the test. Subsequently, the fracture surface was investigated with a Tescan-Vega-II scanning electron microscope (SEM) (Tescan GmbH, Dortmund, Germany). For comparison of the different fracture regions and batches, images near the initial notch and the residual fracture were taken.
L503: ## 3 Results and Discussion
L504: For the long-term and reliable use of recycled PP in demanding technical applications such as in the civil engineering or the automotive industries, information on only the basic parameters like melt flow rate (MFR) and density ρ is insufficient. Instead, mechanical properties and crack resistance are critical.

L626: The morphology of the material and filler content are key factors influencing the crack resistance [【126†54】, 【130†80】-【131†82】]. With regard to the results of the MFR, it can be observed that materials with a comparatively low MFR exhibit increased resistance against fatigue loads [【132†83】]. However, the additional filler content should be considered in this assumption, as a low crack resistance is observed for B1, despite its low MFR value.
L627: In particular, B1 and B9, each containing more than 20% talc, exhibit significantly lower crack resistance. This aligns with literature findings that high talc content decreases crack resistance and reduces the material's ability to plastically deform [【126†54】, 【102†65】]. Interestingly, B5 also demonstrates low crack resistance, despite having the lowest filler content, as indicated by ρ, TGA, and E. The slope is similar to the filled batches B1 and B9.
L628: This flattening in B5 could be attributed to a higher amount of random PP or PE impurities, which lower crystallinity and T_{M}. In contrast to B1, B10 has a slightly higher MFR value but a comparable molecular weight according to the cross-over frequency. The main difference is the filler. B10 contains mostly CaCO_{3} as a filler instead of talc (B1). This filler, CaCO_{3}, apparently has no significant negative influence on the crack resistance.
L629: Observations of B7 reveal that, despite its significantly higher toughness in tensile and Charpy impact tests, it performs similarly to B6 and B8 in the cyclic CRB test. These materials differed only minimally in total filler content (CaCO_{3} and talc) and MFR value, B6 (17.5%, 8.6 g/10 min), B7 (17.9%, 10.6 g/10 min), and B8 (16.4%, 11.3 g/10 min). The results highlight the complexity of determining or predicting the crack resistance of recycled materials.
L630: This is caused, among other factors, by the complex interaction of various influencing factors, making it difficult to directly compare the batches. Another characteristic feature of the results is the high scatter of the measured specimens for a batch, particularly for batches B1 to B5 and B10. This underlines the challenges in interpreting the data and the high sensitivity. While comparatively consistent results were obtained for B7, B8, and B9, other batches have considerable scatter.
L631: Optical analyses using light microscopy and SEM were unable to identify any clear causes or impurities for the high scatter within one batch.
L632: Additional information on the crack resistance of the batches was obtained by a detailed SEM analysis of the fracture surfaces. In (Figure 【133†10】) a fracture surface of B1, with the different regions where the additional SEM images were taken, is illustrated. For comparison, SEM images of a highly talc filled batch (B1) and a batch with low filler content (B5) at the same magnification of 2 kx, near the initial notch as well as from the residual fracture, are presented in (Figure 【134†11】).
L633: It is clearly recognizable that B1 has a significantly higher amount of plate-shaped talc particles, resulting in a different fracture surface. While the fracture surface of B5 appears comparatively smooth, B1 show a pronounced formation, with talc plates embedded in the matrix. The work by Schöne et al. [【102†65】] demonstrates that not only the talc content, but also the quality, size and aspect ratio of the particles have an influence on the crack resistance and mechanical properties.
L634: This could be also the case in this study, as B1 has significant larger talc particles than B5, which, in addition to the talc content, probably has an influence on the mechanical performance. The residual fracture surface is smooth for both batches, the high amount of talc in B1 is still visible.

L645: In summary, the mechanical properties and the crack resistance of the batches are essentially determined by the polymer structure, molecular chain length, crystallinity, impurities, PP grades ratio, and filler shape, size, and content. However, this behavior is not equally pronounced in all batches, which indicates a complex interaction of the various influencing factors.
L646: Particularly noteworthy is the toughness of B7, which is assumed to result from a specific PP composition incorporating ethylene segments that enhance ductility. The broad variation of the batches also highlights that the basic material characterization usually performed on recyclates is not sufficient to identify all influencing factors, underlying mechanisms, or interactions between these factors.

L673: Calculation of CV was carried out by relating the standard deviation to the mean value and converting it into a percentage. This enables a direct comparison of the scatter of the different parameters and describes the relative scatter of the values in relation to the mean value. The higher the CV value, the higher the variation of the batches.
L674: Values for CV range from 0.7% to 175.2%. Particularly high variation was found for η_{0} and ω_{talc}, which also indicates significant differences in the material composition between the batches. These variations can affect the mechanical performance to varying degrees. Mechanical properties such as E and σ_{y}, on the other hand, show a relatively low scatter (CV < 10%), while ε_{b} varies more.
L675: Whereas ΔK_{N = 1E6} exhibited only minor variations due to its narrower range, N_{ΔK = 0.6} shows the highest variations among all the parameters investigated. This observation aligns with literature, indicating that the CRB test is highly sensitive to molecular and morphological changes as well as to filler content [【132†83】].
L676: The results of this work demonstrate that numerous influencing factors on the material behavior and mechanical performance can be identified. At the same time, however, it is apparent that many other influencing factors are not sufficiently captured in recyclates by these standard and quick analysis methods used in this study. The materials used in this study were selected solely based on MFR and ρ.
L677: Although all batches, except for B2, fall within the specified MFR limits, the ten batches still exhibit a considerable variation in their material properties. As a result, ordering materials based on these two parameters alone can lead to significant differences in material quality and finally also in product quality. Consequently, it is necessary to define the material specifications between the manufacturer and supplier in a more precise manner.
L678: A limitation to MFR and ρ is not sufficient to reliably reflect the actual material properties. Defining tolerance ranges narrower and considering additional characteristic parameters would therefore be a great advantage for both quality assurance and the predictability of product properties.
L679: However, in order to fulfill these requirements at all, it is also necessary to improve the treatment process for recyclates, especially in terms of sorting. A more precise sorting according to polymer type and processing grade is the basis for achieving a more consistent material quality and ensuring the desired process and application reliability in the industrial use of recyclates [【53†18】, 【59†21】].
L680: ## 4 Conclusion
L681: The comprehensive characterization of ten batches of a post-consumer polypropylene (PP) recyclate with identical industrial specification regarding melt flow rate (MFR) (7–13 g/10 min) and density (0.97 ± 0.03 g/cm^{3}) has revealed that considerable variations in material occur despite compliance with the specifications. Only one batch missed the required MFR range with 6.1 g/10 min.
L682: Nevertheless, there were considerable variations in rheological and thermal properties, and most importantly, mechanical performance and crack resistance.
L683: The high variation of filler content from 2% to 24% was particularly striking, with calcium carbonate and talc detected in varying quantities and sizes. This not only affects the processability but also has a direct impact on the mechanical performance and crack resistance.
L684: While the Young's modulus and the yield stress remained relatively stable, the impact strength and notch impact strength varied considerably between 47–111 kJ/m^{2} and 2.8–5.4 kJ/m^{2} respectively, as well as the elongation at break (10%–100%), which indicates a broad variation in toughness. For the cyclic crack round bar test, the variations were even more pronounced.
L685: The number of cycles until failure at the same stress intensity factor varied between 3000 and 6.52 million cycles, which corresponds to a factor of > 2000. Accordingly, the test time ranged from less than 10 min to over 15 days, reflecting a difference that, in practice, distinguishes between products with a short and a long service life.
L686: These huge variations in the batches can be attributed to a variety of influencing factors, including differences in the molecular structure, the type and quantity of fillers and the presence of polymeric impurities like different types of polypropylenes, polyethylene, or ethylene vinyl alcohol copolymer. These factors interact in complex ways with each other that simple test methods cannot represent.
L687: Therefore, a simple prediction of material properties based on a few parameters, such as MFR and density, is not appropriate. Additionally, the fact that seasonal influences could not be assessed due to a lack of information underlines the challenges in tracing and assessing quality variations.
L688: Based on the results, it is therefore necessary to expand existing analysis methods to include additional parameters that better reflect the actual performance of the recyclates. In particular, the requirements for recycled materials in terms of mechanical performance should be defined more precisely in order to increase the quality and reliability of recycled products in industrial application.
L689: The treatment and sorting process must be further developed using technologically advanced and material-specific methods to enable more precise separation to minimize the negative impact on material quality.
